agent_reason: Both deliver home-based medical equipment and supplies (sleep, respiratory, diabetes, wound care, urology/ostomy) directly to patients' homes, working with insurers and providers. Same products and same customers.

Both are holding companies of many autonomous specialty commercial P&C insurance businesses selling coverage to businesses. Same product (specialty commercial P&C insurance) and same customers (commercial insureds). The target's resort sale is not a material separate business.

Both make instrumentation and test and measurement products for industrial and medical/healthcare customers, and both are global multi-business industrial technology groups. AMETEK also has a material electromechanical business (motors, interconnects, specialty metals, thermal management) and aerospace/defense and research markets, with no match shown at Fortive. Fortive adds a software and healthcare sterilization/safety emphasis that AMETEK does not show. The overlap is partial on both product and customers, and the target's multi-business scope caps the grade at 1.

Both operate accredited degree-granting universities for working adults, with nursing and healthcare education as a core line (APEI's Rasmussen and Hondros vs. Covista's Chamberlain). Both serve US students online and on campus. APEI adds a military-focused online university, and Covista adds medical and veterinary schools. The nursing and working-adult overlap is strong enough for a direct peer.

Both operate accredited, primarily online universities giving degree programs to working adult students (APEI's American Public University and AMU; Phoenix's University of Phoenix). Same offering and same core customers, with employer partnerships on both sides. APEI adds a military focus and nursing campuses, which is a difference in emphasis rather than a different business.

The target lines only call APi a provider of "safety and specialty services" with "life safety and security services" and OSHA-related programs. They don't show fire protection, HVAC, or who the customers are. Limbach is clearly an MEP/HVAC contractor and maintainer for building owners. Any overlap in HVAC or fire protection, or in customer type, is not shown in the target lines.

Both are branch-based, fleet-owning providers serving construction job sites. The target sells operated concrete pumping and concrete waste services. Herc rents a broad range of equipment, which includes pumps and concrete and masonry gear, mostly without operators. The customers overlap, but the offering is only partly the same and Herc is far broader.

Butler National is mainly an aerospace holding company (aircraft modifications, avionics, defense electronics) and also has a casino management segment (Boot Hill Casino). Full House Resorts only develops, owns and operates regional casinos. It overlaps with just the gaming and hospitality segment of the target. It has none of the aerospace business, so the several-businesses cap of 1 applies.

Both are multi-subsidiary civil and site development contractors. Cardinal self-performs grading, utilities and paving for residential, commercial, industrial and municipal clients. Sterling's E-infrastructure solutions do large-scale site development for commercial and industrial developers. Its Transportation Solutions cover roads and highways, and its Building Solutions cover residential and commercial concrete work. The product overlap (site development, paving and roadwork) and the customer overlap (private developers and public owners) are both real. Sterling is broader, with more heavy civil and data-center work, and it works in different regions, but neither difference removes the core overlap.

Both are active investment managers selling fund products (including active ETFs) and investment management to investors, earning fees on managed assets. Cohen & Steers focuses on real assets and alternative income. Gabelli is a research-driven manager with value, growth and thematic strategies. The product type and investor base overlap. The difference in investment focus is a specialization difference, not a different business.

Both are global active asset managers selling investment strategies through funds, active ETFs and managed accounts. Federated Hermes is broader, with money market, fixed income and equity. It also offers real estate and infrastructure private market solutions, which overlap with Cohen & Steers' real assets focus. Both earn fees on managed assets. The shown lines do not describe customers directly. The customer match rests on both being active managers of investment funds, so it is inferred.

Both are senior-expert, project-based consulting firms serving corporations and similar client types worldwide. CRA sells economic, financial and strategic consulting, mainly for litigation, antitrust and regulatory work. Exponent sells scientific and engineering consulting, such as failure analysis, product risk and health sciences. The business model is the same, but the offerings differ in discipline, and the customer overlap is only partly shown. That makes them adjacent.

Both sell risk management solutions to employers and organizations. CorVel is a claims and managed care service provider (bill review, pharmacy, case management). The shown Gallagher lines describe an insurance broker and risk and benefits consultant. No shown Gallagher line confirms claims administration. The customers overlap but the core offering and revenue mechanism differ, so this is adjacent.

Both are regulated electric and gas utilities that deliver power and gas to retail utility customers. Con Edison also has steam and a transmission investment arm, and Black Hills also generates power. Their territories differ, but the product and customer type are the same.

Both develop land into residential homesites, so the product overlaps. Forestar is a single-line, national lot developer working across 65 markets in 24 states. St. Joe is a Northwest Florida land owner and asset manager that also sells homes and leases commercial property. The shown lines do not confirm that the customers match. Overlap is partial, so the grade is 1.

Both are multi-brand apparel and accessories brand owners (G-III with 30+ licensed and owned brands; Oxford with a house of premium lifestyle brands), so the product overlap is real. The shown lines do not establish the customer mix. G-III stresses design, sourcing and a diversified distribution network. Oxford presents itself as a parent and steward of premium lifestyle brands, with no wholesale or direct-to-consumer detail in the shown lines. G-III's licensed and mass-market breadth also differs from Oxford's premium, owned-brand focus. Same product with unconfirmed customer overlap gives adjacent.

WEX Benefits directly overlaps HealthEquity: HSAs, FSAs, COBRA and benefits administration sold to employers. But WEX is mainly a fleet fuel card and corporate payments company, and those are material businesses today. The target is a pure-play HSA and consumer-directed benefits provider. The several-businesses cap therefore applies, so the score is at most 1.

Both are regional supermarket chains selling groceries and pharmacy services to household shoppers through their own stores. Ingles is in the Southeast and Weis is in the Mid-Atlantic. The two regions do not overlap, but the product and customer match holds. The target's milk plant and real-estate arms are not shown in any target line, so they are ignored.

Both are asset-based North American truckload carriers selling freight transport to shippers across the US, Canada and Mexico. J.B. Hunt is a multi-business, mode-neutral provider: intermodal, dedicated, brokerage/third-party capacity, LTL, final-mile and a 360 digital platform. Marten's shown evidence is mainly refrigerated, dry van and OTR truckload with cross-border service. The overlap is in truckload and OTR freight, but Marten does not show J.B. Hunt's other material lines, and its refrigerated focus is narrower. Adjacent, not direct.

Both are homebuilders that build and sell new homes directly to individual homebuyers. NVR also has mortgage banking and title arms, but homebuilding is its core. Meritage's shown lines are about new homes for buyers and the homebuilding process.

Both are national homebuilders selling single-family homes, townhomes and condos to individual homebuyers, with affiliated mortgage and title/settlement services supporting home sales. Same product and same customers.

Both own and operate wired and fiber networks. They sell broadband, cable TV and voice to residential and business customers. LICT also sells wholesale carrier access, and Shentel's evidence shows business services. The two sell the same services to the same customer types. They differ mainly in geography: Shentel serves VA, WV, KY and MD, and LICT serves rural areas in other states.

Both are regional wireline operators that sell fiber internet, TV and phone to residential households and also sell business services. Both are expanding fiber with state government broadband programs. The only clear difference is geography: Shentel serves the Mid-Atlantic and Appalachia, and Nuvera serves southern Minnesota and northern Iowa.

Both sell cloud software to small local service businesses (home services, health and similar), so customers match. Thryv is also a done-for-you marketing services provider and a print and online directory seller (Yellowpages.com, Superpages.com). EverCommerce matches only the SaaS part. It adds payment acceptance and several vertical SaaS lines. Thryv has other material businesses today, so the grade is capped at 1.
